guide.title: Reading a delivery receipt
guide.subtitle: What a status actually tells you, and what it does not
guide.excerpt: A receipt is a sequence of states, not a verdict. Treating an intermediate one as final is the most common way a sending dashboard ends up lying to you.

p: When a provider accepts a message, all it has confirmed is that the request was well-formed and the provider has taken responsibility for it. The handset has not been reached. Delivery happens later, asynchronously, and arrives as a separate event.
These are different facts and they belong in different columns. A dashboard that shows accepted messages as delivered is not being optimistic; it is reporting something that has not happened yet.

A message commonly passes through a queued state, a sent or submitted state, and finally a delivered or failed state. Some providers also emit states that are only meaningful while a message is being retried.

The intermediate states are informational. Only the terminal outcome should be used to decide whether a message arrived, and a system that promotes an intermediate state to a terminal one will produce numbers that are wrong in the direction of looking better than reality.

Each provider reports statuses in its own vocabulary. The platform maps them into one shared set so that the same outcome reads the same way regardless of which provider handled the message, and keeps the raw provider code alongside so nothing is lost in the translation.
The practical effect is that a failure reason is comparable across providers, while a provider-specific error still has a code you can hand to that provider support team verbatim.

Receipts are not only a dashboard concern. The platform can forward them to an endpoint you control, so delivery outcomes can drive your own systems — a retry, a support ticket, a customer notification.
sections.scope: Delivery receipt collection and forwarding are implemented for the SMS channel. Email and WhatsApp receipts are not implemented for those channels today.
